analysis.one_liner: Bans PFAS 'forever chemicals' in food packaging like wrappers and takeout containers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with one Republican cosponsor, has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee since July 2026 with no hearing or vote; it dies unless the committee acts before the Congress ends in January 2027.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill amends federal food safety law to make it illegal to sell food packaging — things like fast-food wrappers, pizza boxes, and takeout containers — that contains intentionally added PFAS, a class of long-lasting chemicals used to repel grease and water. The ban would take effect January 1, 2027. PFAS are called 'forever chemicals' because they do not break down and have been linked in research to health problems; they migrate from packaging into food. The bill went nowhere: it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, and no further action appears in the record.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who eat packaged and restaurant food — nearly everyone — would get less PFAS exposure from grease-proofing coatings migrating into their food. Food-service and packaging companies that already make PFAS-free alternatives would gain a level national playing field instead of a patchwork of state bans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone who eats packaged or restaurant food

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a prohibited act under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to introduce into interstate commerce food packaging containing intentionally added PFAS, effective January 1, 2027.
Defines PFAS broadly as any fluorinated organic chemical containing at least one fully fluorinated methyl or methylene carbon atom, closing off easy chemical-by-chemical loopholes.

PFAS do not break down in the body or environment and can migrate from food-contact materials into food, so removing them at the packaging source reduces exposure for people who cannot shop their way around it.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of paper and paperboard food packaging that uses PFAS grease-proofing coatings, and the restaurants and food-service chains that buy their products, would bear the cost of switching to PFAS-free alternatives. The cost shows up partly in packaging prices passed to consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: PFAS-using packaging makers and food-service buyers

drawbacks.text: Compliance cost: packaging makers would need to reformulate or switch suppliers of grease-resistant coatings before the January 1, 2027 effective date, which is a short runway for companies with long supply contracts.

A good-faith objection is that the ban sweeps in the entire class of chemicals at once rather than restricting specific PFAS compounds proven to migrate into food, which industry would argue overreaches relative to the demonstrated risk of any single compound.
The bill sets a federal floor but includes no funding for enforcement or testing, so its real-world effect would depend on FDA inspection capacity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — less exposure to persistent chemicals through everyday food packaging — is broad and durable, and substitutes already exist since several states have enacted similar bans, which keeps the compliance cost moderate. The main weakness is the abrupt effective date and the lack of enforcement resources, not the principle of the ban.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on July 6, 2026 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the same day, where it has remained without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Debbie Dingell introduced the Keep Food Containers Safe from PFAS Act of 2026 on July 6, 2026, joined by Representative Brian Fitzpatrick as its sole cosponsor.

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction, and the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action.
The bill text would amend the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to prohibit food packaging containing intentionally added PFAS beginning January 1, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has been forced to change: packaging manufacturers that still use PFAS coatings continue to sell into the national market, and nothing in the record shows the committee planning to act before the Congress ends in January 2027.

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sent it to committee.

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it bipartisan at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 6, 2026 and took no action on it; the chair never scheduled a hearing or markup.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan at introduction — a Democratic sponsor with one Republican cosponsor — but no votes have occurred, so the partisan shape of any final decision is unknown.

industries.note: The bill bans their grease-proofing chemistry outright from January 1, 2027, forcing reformulation or supplier changes. Their continued sales of PFAS-coated packaging put the chemicals into food that ordinary people eat.
Companies that already sell PFAS-free grease-resistant packaging would gain customers as buyers must switch, and a national rule ends the patchwork of state-level bans.

They would face switching costs on wrappers, boxes, and bowls, but a single national standard simplifies compliance with state bans many chains already navigate, and reduces PFAS in their own products.
Chemical makers supplying fluorinated grease-proofing agents would lose the food-contact market segment the bill defines broadly enough to cover their product class.

analysis.trajectory: The Congress ends January 3, 2027. With one cosponsor, no committee hearing or markup four months after referral, and the bill's effective date (January 1, 2027) already inside the session, the likely path is that the bill dies in committee at the end of the Congress unless the Energy and Commerce Committee unexpectedly schedules it. A companion could be refiled in the next Congress.
